ev.q: This report provides an update on the progress made in COVID-19 vaccination in the African Region during 2021–2023.
COVID-19 Vaccination Coverage — World Health Organization African Region, 2021–2023
This report provides an update on the progress made in COVID-19 vaccination in the African Region during 2021–2023.
Four (9%) of the 47 countries in the region achieved the WHO target of 70% primary series coverage in the total population in 2022
Countries were requested to report weekly on the number of COVID-19 vaccine doses received from all sources and the number of doses administered.
These data were compiled in the African Region regional database.

equity.level_reason: The only SPD is age (older age groups, ≥50 years, as a WHO priority group), reported without social-position framing. Disparities in vaccine access are framed between low-income countries, which is geography or country income group, not an SPD.

level_alternative.reason: Vaccine access disparities for low-income countries could be read as an SES framing raised as context, though country income group is excluded as an SPD.

ev.q: Among 22 countries reporting data on older populations, primary series coverage was 52%.
Older age group definition varies from country to country, but aged ≥50 years.

equity.equity_measurement: Inequity is framed between countries (vaccine access for low-income countries), which is geography, not an SPD. Health care workers are an occupational priority group, not SES. Total population is the denominator despite differing eligible ages.

notes: Coverage is computed by division from administrative dose counts; no tests, CIs or models. Design inferred: monitoring progress against the WHO 70% target, plus descriptive surveillance. Country-level coverage is compared side by side and against 70%/40% thresholds.
view_issues: The Abstract gives 38% with ≥1 dose, but Results give 440 million (37%). The Discussion says four countries reached the 70% target 'in 2022' while Table 2 is cumulative to December 2023. Footnote § calls the eligible population 'the numerator', which seems wrong.
